topic: Back to uni: laptops, backpacks and long lectures

slides.headline: Uni's back. Is your body ready?
slides.sub: Laptops, backpacks and three-hour lectures: small changes that help.

slides.title: Lift the laptop in the library
slides.body: Hunching over a laptop on a low desk for hours tends to load the neck and upper back. Prop it on a few books and plug in a cheap separate keyboard for longer study sessions.

slides.title: Two straps beat one
slides.body: One strap is fine for a short walk. For a long trek across campus, use both straps, pack heavy items close to your back and leave behind what you won't need that day.

slides.title: Break up the long lectures
slides.body: Two or three hours in a lecture seat is a long time to stay still. Shift position often, stand at the break and take the stairs between classes. Small movement snacks add up.

slides.title: Timetable your training
slides.body: Exercise is often the first thing dropped when uni gets busy. Book two short strength or sport sessions into your week like a class, so they survive assignment season.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading into an arm or leg, pins and needles, numbness, or pain that keeps building over a few weeks despite changes is worth an assessment rather than a guess.

slides.headline: Studying with a sore neck?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios look at how you sit, carry and move, then build a simple plan around your timetable. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Back at uni and already stiff by week two? 🎒

February brings full timetables, long lectures and hours bent over a laptop in the library. Bodies usually cope well with all of that. What they struggle with is the same position for hours, plus a heavy bag slung over one shoulder.

A few small changes go a long way: lift your laptop and add a separate keyboard, use both backpack straps on longer walks, move at every lecture break, and lock two short training sessions into your timetable.

Pain that spreads into an arm or leg, pins and needles, or pain that keeps building is worth getting checked. Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios see plenty of students. Book online via the link in bio.

topic: Massage for martial arts and BJJ training

slides.headline: Rolling five nights a week?
slides.sub: How remedial massage can fit around BJJ and martial arts training.

slides.title: Grip, neck and hips work hard
slides.body: Gripping gis, framing, bridging and holding guard load the forearms, neck, upper back and hips heavily. Those are often the areas that feel tight and heavy after a big training week.

slides.title: What massage can realistically offer
slides.body: Remedial massage can help you feel less tight and move more comfortably between sessions. It's a complement to good training, sleep and strength work, not a replacement for them.

slides.title: Time it around training
slides.body: Lighter work a day or two before a competition or grading usually sits better than firm pressure. Save deeper sessions for a lighter training day, and tell your therapist what's coming up.

slides.title: Tell your therapist about the mat
slides.body: Let your therapist know your style, how often you train, and any recent joint locks you tapped late on or awkward landings. It helps them choose areas, pressure and positions that suit you.

slides.title: When massage isn't the answer
slides.body: A joint that feels unstable, a pop with swelling, numbness or tingling, or a knock to the head needs a proper assessment rather than a massage. Our physiotherapists can help with that.

topic: Back gadgets: massage guns, inversion tables and more

slides.headline: Back gadgets: what they can and can't do
slides.sub: Massage guns, inversion tables and braces, kept in perspective.

slides.title: Massage guns: short-term relief
slides.body: Many people find a massage gun eases tightness for a while. Keep it on muscle rather than bone, start on a low setting, and avoid the front of the neck and any numb areas.

slides.title: Inversion tables: be cautious
slides.body: Hanging upside down isn't suitable for everyone. Blood pressure, eye, heart or other health conditions and pregnancy can all be reasons to avoid it. Check with your GP or practitioner first.

slides.title: Posture braces: a reminder only
slides.body: A brace can act as a cue to change position, but most people don't need to wear one for hours. Moving often and building upper back strength usually matter more.

slides.title: Movement does the heavy lifting
slides.body: No gadget replaces regular walking, strength work and staying active. Heat packs and rollers can be a handy warm-up for exercise, rather than the whole plan.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain with leg numbness or weakness, pain that keeps building over weeks, or changes to bladder or bowel control need a proper assessment, the last one promptly.

slides.headline: Not sure what's worth using?
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess your back, talk through what you use at home and combine adjustments with exercise and practical advice. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Got a massage gun in the cupboard and still a stiff back?

Back gadgets can be handy. A massage gun or heat pack often eases tightness for a while, and a brace can remind you to change position. They tend to be most useful as a warm-up or a cue to move, not as the whole plan.

Inversion tables deserve extra caution. They aren't suitable for everyone, especially with blood pressure, eye or heart conditions, or during pregnancy, so check with your GP or practitioner before trying one.

topic: Pilates for knee osteoarthritis

slides.body: Lying down and pressing the carriage away lets you strengthen thighs and hips with less body weight through the knee. Springs and range can be adjusted as you go.

slides.title: Some knee feedback is normal
slides.body: Mild aching during or after exercise is common with knee osteoarthritis and usually settles within a day. If your knee is much worse the next morning, say so and the plan gets adjusted.

slides.title: Build towards standing work
slides.body: Over the weeks, sessions often add standing work like step-ups, sit-to-stands and balance, so the strength carries over to stairs, walking and getting out of the car.

slides.title: When to get it checked

topic: Mallet finger in ball sports

slides.headline: Fingertip won't straighten after a catch?
slides.sub: Mallet finger is common in ball sports. Here's what usually happens next.

slides.title: What mallet finger is
slides.body: A ball hitting the tip of a straight finger can injure the tendon that straightens the last joint, sometimes with a small flake of bone. The fingertip then droops and can't lift on its own.

slides.title: Get it looked at early
slides.body: See a GP, physiotherapist or hand therapist soon after the injury rather than waiting to see if it settles. An X-ray is often used, and early splinting is usually the main treatment.

slides.title: The splint stays on
slides.body: The fingertip is usually kept straight in a splint, day and night, for a period set by your doctor. Letting it bend can set things back, so splint changes and skin care need care.

slides.title: Keep the rest of the hand moving
slides.body: While the tip is splinted, gently moving the other finger joints, wrist and shoulder helps limit stiffness. Your physio can show you how to clean the skin and swap splints safely.

slides.title: Back to ball sports
slides.body: Return to play is usually gradual, often with protective taping or a splint during games for a while. Timing depends on your injury and what your doctor or surgeon advises.

slides.headline: Fingertip drooping after a game?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios can assess your finger, work with your GP and guide splinting and your return to sport. Book online — link in bio.

topic: Hurt doesn't always mean harm

slides.headline: Sore during rehab? How to read it
slides.sub: Pain is a protector, not a damage meter. A simple way to judge it.

slides.title: Pain is a protector
slides.body: Your nervous system produces pain to protect you. It responds to sleep, stress, worry and past experience as well as load on your tissues, so the volume isn't always a measure of damage.

slides.title: Use a 0 to 10 guide
slides.body: During exercise, pain up to about 3 or 4 out of 10 that settles soon after is often acceptable in rehab. Your practitioner can set the number that suits your situation.

slides.title: Check the next morning
slides.body: If you're back to your usual baseline by the next morning, the load was likely fine. If things are noticeably worse, ease back a step rather than stopping everything.

slides.title: Adjust, don't abandon
slides.body: Change one thing at a time: fewer reps, less weight, a smaller range or more rest between sets. Most people keep progressing with small tweaks rather than complete rest.

slides.title: When pain means get checked
slides.body: Sudden severe pain, new swelling, a joint giving way, numbness or weakness, fever, or night pain that doesn't ease with rest are signs to get assessed.

slides.headline: Not sure how hard to push?
slides.body: Our team can help you understand your pain and set clear limits for exercise and daily life. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
A twinge during exercise doesn't automatically mean you've made things worse.

Pain is your body's protection system, and it's influenced by sleep, stress and past experience as well as what your tissues are doing. That's why it isn't a reliable damage meter on its own.

A practical approach many rehab programs use: mild pain during exercise, often up to 3 or 4 out of 10, that settles soon after is usually okay. Then check the next morning. Back to baseline? Carry on. Noticeably worse? Ease back one step instead of stopping completely.

topic: Walking lunges: knee-friendly tips

slides.headline: Walking lunges making your knees grumble?
slides.sub: A few setup tweaks that often make lunges feel smoother.

slides.title: Find your stride length
slides.body: A short, cramped step pushes the front knee well forward. A slightly longer stride shares the work with your hip. Aim for a length where you feel balanced, not stretched.

slides.title: Knees past toes is okay
slides.body: Your knee travelling past your toes is normal for most people. If your knee is sensitive for now, a small forward lean from the hips can shift some load towards your glutes.

slides.title: Control the way down
slides.body: Lower for two or three seconds rather than dropping onto the back knee. Slow control on the way down builds strength and tends to feel smoother for sensitive knees.

slides.title: Shrink the range first
slides.body: If full depth is sore, stop halfway or hold a rail. Reverse lunges or split squats on the spot are often easier, then build back towards walking lunges over a few weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Knee swelling, locking or giving way, or pain that lingers for days after training, is worth an assessment rather than pushing through every session and hoping it settles.

slides.headline: Want lunges that feel solid?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios can watch your lunge, tweak your setup and build a plan for your knees. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Walking lunges on every preseason program, and your knees aren't keen?

Lunges are a great exercise for legs and hips, and knees are usually well able to handle them. A few tweaks often make them feel much smoother.

Try a slightly longer stride, lower slowly for two or three seconds, and don't stress about your knee going past your toes. If full depth is sore, shorten the range or switch to reverse lunges or split squats on the spot, then build back up.

topic: Massage for hairdressers and barbers

slides.headline: Behind the chair all day?
slides.sub: Hairdressers and barbers: where the load builds and what can help.

slides.title: Arms up, head tilted
slides.body: Holding scissors, clippers and dryers near shoulder height for hours loads the shoulders, upper back and neck. Forearms and thumbs also work hard with repeated gripping and fine cutting.

slides.title: Pump the chair to your height
slides.body: Raise or lower the client's chair so you're working around chest height, and step around them rather than leaning or reaching. Small adjustments add up over a long day.

slides.title: Mini-breaks between clients
slides.body: Between appointments, drop your arms, roll your shoulders, shake out your hands and gently stretch your forearms. Thirty seconds each time can ease the build-up.

slides.title: Where massage fits
slides.body: Remedial massage can ease tight shoulders, neck and forearms and help you feel looser after a busy week. It works well alongside breaks and strength work, not instead of them.

slides.title: When to see a physio
slides.body: Numbness or tingling in the fingers, hand weakness, dropping tools, or pain that keeps building despite changes is worth a physio assessment rather than massage alone.

topic: Back pain in tall people: furniture that fits

slides.headline: Too tall for your desk and car?
slides.sub: Practical tweaks when standard furniture wasn't built for your height.

slides.title: Raise the desk, not your shoulders
slides.body: Standard desks are often low for tall people, so you end up hunched. Use desk risers or a sit-stand desk set near elbow height, and lift your screen so the top sits around eye level.

slides.title: Chair depth and height matter
slides.body: A short seat leaves your thighs unsupported. Look for a deeper seat, raise it so your hips sit level with or a little above your knees, and add a lumbar cushion if it helps.

slides.title: Car seat: back and down
slides.body: Slide the seat back, lower it if headroom is tight and keep the backrest fairly upright. Set the steering wheel and mirrors so you aren't craning forward on longer drives.

slides.title: Low benches and sinks
slides.body: Bending to low benches adds up for tall people. Hinge from your hips, rest one foot on a cupboard ledge, or raise the chopping board on a sturdy box for longer tasks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Leg numbness or weakness and pain that keeps building over weeks are worth getting assessed. Changes to bladder or bowel control need prompt medical attention.

slides.body: Our chiropractors look at how you sit, drive and work, using adjustments alongside exercise and practical setup advice. Book online — link in bio.

slides.title: Start below what you think
slides.body: After a long break, early sessions should feel easy. Starting well below your old level gives joints, tendons and muscles time to adapt, and makes coming back next week more likely.

slides.title: Expect some muscle soreness
slides.body: Mild soreness a day or two after a new session is common and usually eases within a few days. It's usually a sign your body is adapting, not that something is wrong.

slides.title: Twice a week is plenty
slides.body: Two sessions a week is a realistic starting rhythm for most people. Add a couple of walks in between and you have a simple routine that fits around work and family.

slides.title: Check with your GP first if
slides.body: If you have a heart or lung condition, get chest pain or dizziness with effort, or have a health condition you're unsure about, check with your GP before starting a new routine.

topic: Ankle mobility and squat depth

slides.headline: Heels lifting when you squat deep?
slides.sub: Your ankles might be the limit. Here's how to check and what helps.

slides.title: Ankles help set your depth
slides.body: As you squat, your knees need to travel forward over your toes. If your ankles don't bend enough, your heels lift, your chest tips forward or you stop short. It's a common, workable limit.

slides.title: Try the knee-to-wall test
slides.body: Kneel facing a wall with your front foot about a hand-width away. Keep the heel down and push your knee to touch the wall. Compare sides. A big difference between ankles is worth noting.

slides.title: Mobilise, then use it
slides.body: Rock your knee forward over your toes for 10 to 15 slow reps, heel down. Then go straight into a few squats so your body practises using the new range under load.

slides.title: Small tweaks while you build
slides.body: A slightly wider stance, toes turned out a touch, or a small plate under your heels can help you squat deeper while your ankle range builds over a few weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: An ankle that has stayed stiff since an old sprain, a pinching pain at the front of the ankle when you squat, or swelling after training is worth an assessment rather than more stretching.

slides.headline: Want deeper, steadier squats?
slides.body: Our physios check your ankles, hips and squat pattern, then give you a short plan to build range you can actually use. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Heels peeling off the floor at the bottom of your squat? Check your ankles before you blame your hips. 🏋️

Squatting deep needs your knees to travel forward over your toes, and that relies on ankle bend. When it runs short, your heels lift, your chest drops forward or you stop early.

Try the knee-to-wall test to compare sides, rock your knee forward for a few slow reps before you squat, and use a slightly wider stance or a small plate under your heels while your range builds. Pinching at the front of the ankle or a stiff ankle since an old sprain is worth getting assessed.

topic: Dead hangs: are they good for your shoulders?

slides.headline: Dead hangs: shoulder saviour or hype?
slides.sub: What hanging can do, who it suits and how to start sensibly.

slides.title: What a dead hang actually is
slides.body: Hanging from a bar with straight arms and your feet off the ground. It works your grip and takes your shoulders into a full overhead position, with body weight adding a gentle stretch.

slides.title: What it can help with
slides.body: Many people use hangs to build grip strength and get comfortable with overhead range. Research on hangs specifically is limited, so treat them as one useful tool rather than a shoulder reset.

slides.title: Start with your feet down
slides.body: Keep your toes on a box or the floor and take some weight through your legs. Hang for 10 to 20 seconds for a few sets, then build time gradually over several weeks.

slides.title: Passive or active hang?
slides.body: A passive hang lets your shoulders rise towards your ears. An active hang gently draws your shoulder blades down. Both have a place, and mixing them builds control as well as range.

slides.title: When to hold off for now
slides.body: Shoulder pain that lingers after hanging, a recent dislocation, pins and needles into the hand, or a shoulder that feels unstable overhead are worth assessing before you hang.

slides.headline: Thinking of adding dead hangs?
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios check your shoulder range and strength, then show you how hangs can fit a sensible program. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Dead hangs are all over your feed. Are they actually good for your shoulders?

For many people, hanging from a bar is a handy way to build grip strength and get used to having the arms overhead. The research on hangs specifically is limited, though, so they're one useful tool rather than an answer to every shoulder problem.

Start with your feet supported on a box, hang for 10 to 20 seconds, and build gradually. Mix passive hangs with active ones where you draw the shoulder blades down. Lingering pain, a recent dislocation or tingling into the hand are reasons to get assessed first.

topic: Massage for dancers' hips and feet

slides.headline: Long rehearsals, aching hips and arches?
slides.sub: Where remedial massage fits into a dancer's recovery week.

slides.title: Where dancers carry the load
slides.body: Turnout, jumps and hours on demi-pointe ask a lot of the deep hip muscles, calves and the small muscles under the foot. Tightness and fatigue there are common through a busy term.

slides.title: What massage can help with
slides.body: Many dancers find massage eases that heavy, tight feeling around the hips, calves and arches. It complements strength work, technique and rest rather than replacing them.

slides.title: Time it around rehearsals
slides.body: Lighter work tends to suit the day before a performance. Deeper work usually feels better on a lighter training day, so your legs have time to settle before a demanding class.

topic: Evening back stiffness after a long day

slides.body: Change position every 30 to 45 minutes. Stand for calls, walk to refill your water and take the stairs. Varying how you load your back through the day often helps more than one long stretch at night.

topic: Tendon pain: why rest alone rarely settles it

slides.headline: Rested your tendon for weeks. Still sore?
slides.sub: Why tendons usually need the right load, not just time off.

slides.title: Tendons respond to load
slides.body: Tendons adapt to the work you give them. Complete rest can ease pain for a while, but it often leaves the tendon less ready for running, lifting or stairs when you return.

slides.title: Calm it, don't stop it
slides.body: Most people do well by reducing the aggravating activity rather than stopping everything. Keep moving within a level of discomfort that has settled by the next morning.

slides.title: Start with steady holds
slides.body: Slow, sustained holds, like holding a calf raise at the top or a wall sit, are often a good starting point. They tend to be well tolerated and begin rebuilding capacity.

slides.title: Build up gradually
slides.body: Over weeks, progress to slow heavy lifts, then faster, springier work like hopping. Research suggests tendons change slowly, so most programs run for months rather than days.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A sudden pop or sharp pain followed by weakness, a lot of swelling, or tendon pain that keeps getting worse despite changes is worth an assessment promptly.

slides.body: Going from a summer off to three hard sessions a week is a big jump. Research suggests sharp increases in training load are linked with more soft tissue niggles.

slides.body: Increase your total running gradually, adding a little distance or one extra session at a time. Every third or fourth week, ease back slightly to let your body catch up.

slides.title: Prepare for sprints early
slides.body: Hamstrings are often the first to complain. Include some fast running early in preseason at lower volumes, plus strength work like bridges and Nordics, rather than saving sprints for later.

slides.title: Change of direction counts
slides.body: Cutting, stepping and tackling load your knees and ankles differently from straight running. Add agility drills progressively, starting slower and building speed over a few weeks.

slides.body: A sudden sharp pain in the back of the thigh, a knee that gives way, or pain that builds through each session rather than easing is worth a physio assessment.

slides.title: Most of life is single-leg
slides.body: Walking, stairs, running, stepping out of a car: you're mostly on one leg at a time. Training both legs together is useful, but it can hide a side that's quietly doing less.

slides.title: Two-leg moves can hide a gap
slides.body: In a squat or leg press, the stronger side often takes a bit more load without you noticing. Working one side at a time shows the difference and gives the quieter side its fair share.

slides.title: Balance comes along for the ride
slides.body: Standing on one leg asks your hip, knee and foot to work as a team. Single-leg footwork on the reformer builds strength and steadiness together, at a load you can control.

slides.body: Single-leg sit-to-stand from a high chair, 6 to 8 per side, holding a bench if needed. Lower the chair or slow the movement as it gets easier. Note which side feels harder.

slides.title: Uneven isn't always a problem
slides.body: Small differences between sides are normal. If one leg is clearly weaker after an injury, or a knee, hip or ankle hurts during single-leg work, it's worth an assessment first.

topic: Pain at the back of the knee

slides.headline: Ache behind your knee?
slides.sub: A few common reasons, and what usually helps.

slides.title: A few usual suspects
slides.body: Pain behind the knee often comes from the hamstring or calf tendons near the joint, a fluid-filled swelling linked to the knee (a Baker's cyst), or a recent jump in activity.

slides.title: Notice what sets it off
slides.body: Is it worse fully straightening, deep squatting, running downhill or after long sits? Jot it down for a week. The pattern helps your physio narrow things down faster.

slides.title: Ease the load, don't stop
slides.body: Most people settle sooner by trimming the aggravating activity rather than resting completely. Shorter runs, flatter routes and a slightly shallower squat often keep you moving while things calm.

slides.title: Strength usually helps
slides.body: Gradual hamstring and calf strengthening, like bridges and heel raises, helps the tissues behind the knee handle more load. Start with what feels comfortable and build over a few weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked promptly
slides.body: Calf swelling, warmth, redness or tenderness, especially after surgery, a long flight or time off your feet, needs prompt medical review with a GP or emergency department. So does a knee that locks.

topic: What progress looks like: it's rarely a straight line

slides.headline: Two good weeks, then a bad day?
slides.sub: Recovery rarely runs in a straight line. That's normal.

slides.title: Expect a few zigzags
slides.body: Most recoveries go up and down. A good week can be followed by a flare-up after a big day, poor sleep or a stressful stretch. The trend over a month matters more than any single day.

slides.title: A flare-up isn't starting over
slides.body: Flare-ups usually settle within a few days with a short step back in load. They rarely mean you've undone your progress. Ease off a little, keep moving, then build up again.

slides.title: Track more than pain
slides.body: Write down what you can do: stairs, sleep, how long you can sit or walk. These often improve before pain does, and show progress a pain score on a bad day can hide.

slides.title: Compare with last month
slides.body: Compare this week with four weeks ago, not with yesterday. If you're doing more overall, you're likely on track, even if today feels flat. Bring your notes to your next appointment.

slides.title: When to check in sooner
slides.body: If you're steadily worse over a couple of weeks, notice new symptoms like numbness or weakness, or the pain feels different from usual, let your practitioner know rather than waiting.

slides.headline: Not sure you're on track?
slides.body: Our team reviews your progress with you and adjusts the plan when things stall or flare. Book online — link in bio.

A few things help: track what you can do, not just how sore you are. Compare this month with last month rather than today with yesterday. After a flare-up, step back a little, keep moving, then build up again.

topic: Sitting on a gym ball at work: worth it?

slides.headline: Swapped your desk chair for a ball?
slides.sub: Does it actually help your back? The short answer.

slides.title: The idea behind it
slides.body: The theory is that a wobbly ball keeps your trunk muscles 'switched on'. Research suggests the difference in muscle activity is small, and most people slump on a ball once they tire.

slides.title: Movement matters more than the seat
slides.body: What tends to help backs at work is changing position often. A ball can encourage small shifts, but so can a regular chair if you get up, walk and stretch regularly.

slides.title: Like it? Use it in short bursts
slides.body: Try 15 to 20 minutes on the ball, then back to a supportive chair. Pump it so your hips sit slightly above your knees, feet flat, and check it's rated for your weight.

slides.title: Weigh up the trade-offs
slides.body: Balls have no backrest or armrests, can roll away when you stand, and often sit at the wrong height for your desk. If your back aches more by afternoon, it may not suit you.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain spreading into a leg, numbness, pins and needles, or pain that keeps building over weeks, whatever you sit on, is worth an assessment rather than another seat swap.

slides.headline: Not sure what suits your desk?
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess how your back moves and combine hands-on care with exercises and simple desk changes. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Thinking of swapping your office chair for a gym ball?

The idea is that an unstable seat keeps your trunk working. Research suggests the extra muscle activity is small, and most people end up slumping once they get tired.

What usually matters more for your back is how often you change position. A ball can nudge you to shift around, and some people simply enjoy it. If that's you, use it in 15 to 20 minute bursts, get the height right, and swap back to a supportive chair.

Pain spreading into a leg, numbness or pain that keeps building is worth an assessment, whatever you're sitting on.

topic: Side planks for a stronger trunk

slides.headline: Side planks: tough, but worth it
slides.sub: A trunk exercise that works your hips too. How to build it.

slides.title: Why go sideways?
slides.body: Side planks load the muscles along the side of your trunk and hip together. These help you carry shopping on one side, change direction in sport and stay steady on one leg.

slides.title: Start on your knees
slides.body: Lie on your side, elbow under shoulder, knees bent. Lift your hips so you're straight from knees to head. Hold 10 to 20 seconds, 3 times each side, breathing normally.

slides.title: Then build up gradually
slides.body: When knee holds feel easy, straighten your legs, staggering your feet for balance. Add time before adding difficulty. Hip dips or a top-leg lift come later, once holds feel steady.

slides.title: Common slips to watch
slides.body: Hips sagging or piking back, the shoulder creeping up to your ear, and holding your breath. A mirror or quick phone video helps. Shorter, cleaner holds usually beat long wobbly ones.

slides.title: When to change it up
slides.body: If your shoulder grumbles, try a version with your hand on a bench. Sharp back pain, or pain spreading into a leg, is worth getting assessed before pushing on.

slides.headline: Want a trunk plan that fits you?
slides.body: Our Chatswood physios work out where to start and how to progress, so trunk work suits your body and goals. Book online — link in bio.

They load the side of your trunk and your hip at the same time, which helps with carrying things on one side, changing direction in sport and balancing on one leg. Handy with winter preseason starting.

Start on your knees, elbow under shoulder, and hold 10 to 20 seconds, 3 times a side. When that feels easy, straighten your legs. Add time before difficulty, and keep holds clean rather than long.

A grumbly shoulder usually just needs a different version. Sharp back pain or pain into a leg is worth getting checked.

topic: The side-lying series: why we do it

slides.headline: Why so much time on your side?
slides.sub: The side-lying series is less boring than it looks.

slides.title: What the series is
slides.body: A run of leg lifts, circles and small kicks done lying on your side. Your trunk and bottom leg stay still while the top leg moves, so the hip muscles do the work.

slides.title: It targets the side of the hip
slides.body: Muscles on the outside of the hip help keep your pelvis level when you walk, run or climb stairs. This series trains them without putting much load through the knees or lower back.

slides.title: Control beats height
slides.body: A high leg lift usually means the waist or pelvis has rolled back to help. Smaller, slower lifts with the hips stacked feel harder and tend to give the hip muscles more to do.

slides.title: Try it against a wall
slides.body: Lie on your side with your back and heels against a wall, knees slightly bent. Lift the top leg 10 times, slowly, keeping the heel touching the wall. Feel the outer hip working.

slides.title: If lying on your side hurts
slides.body: Pressure on the bottom hip can be uncomfortable. A folded towel under it, or a pillow between the knees, often helps. Ongoing pain on the side of the hip is worth an assessment.

caption:

The trick is control. Small, slow lifts with your hips stacked are harder than big swings, and they keep the work where it belongs. Try it with your back against a wall to feel the difference.

If lying on your side is uncomfortable, a towel or pillow usually helps. Ongoing side-of-hip pain is worth an assessment.

topic: Massage for drivers and couriers

slides.headline: Hours driving, then lifting parcels?
slides.sub: Where remedial massage fits for drivers and couriers.

slides.title: Two very different loads
slides.body: Long stretches sitting still, then quick bursts of lifting, twisting and stairs. That mix often shows up as tight hips, a stiff lower back, and a neck and shoulders sore from the wheel.

slides.title: What massage can do
slides.body: Remedial massage can ease muscle tension and help you feel less stiff after a run of shifts. It complements movement and strength work rather than replacing them, and the effects are usually short-term.

slides.title: Common areas to work on
slides.body: Hip flexors and glutes from sitting, the lower back, the neck and upper shoulders from steering, and forearms from gripping. Your therapist will ask about your route and loads first.

slides.title: Small habits on the road
slides.body: At each stop, stand tall and take a few steps before lifting. Roll your shoulders while parked. Keep parcels close to your body and turn your feet rather than twisting.

slides.title: When to see someone else
slides.body: Numbness, pins and needles, pain spreading down a leg or arm, or back pain after a lift that doesn't ease is worth a physio or GP assessment rather than massage alone.

topic: Knee clicking: when it matters

slides.headline: Knees click on the stairs?
slides.sub: Most clicks are harmless. Here's when it's worth a look.

slides.title: Noise on its own is common
slides.body: Many knees click, crack or grind when squatting or climbing stairs. Research suggests painless knee noises are very common and usually aren't a sign of anything harmful happening inside.

slides.title: Symptoms matter more than sound
slides.body: A click that comes with pain, swelling or a catching feeling is different from a noisy but comfortable knee. It's what happens around the sound that tells you more.

slides.title: Don't let the noise slow you
slides.body: Avoiding stairs or squats because of a click can leave your legs less conditioned. Most noisy knees cope well with everyday use, so keep moving and build up gradually.

slides.title: Strength often helps
slides.body: For noisy, mildly achy knees, gradual quad, hip and calf strength work often helps them feel more confident. Sit-to-stands and step-ups are a good starting point, three times a week.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Clicking with swelling after activity, pain that's getting worse, a knee that locks or gives way, or noise that started with a twist or injury is worth a physio assessment.

topic: Watching weekend sport from the sidelines: back care

slides.headline: Long day on the sidelines?
slides.sub: Back care for parents and fans at weekend sport.

slides.title: Why spectating gets to your back
slides.body: Standing on hard ground, perching on low folding chairs, leaning on fences and hours in the car between games. It isn't strenuous, but staying in one position often leaves backs stiff.

slides.title: Choose your seat with care
slides.body: A chair with a backrest, with hips level with or slightly above your knees, is usually kinder than a low beach chair. A folded towel on a deep seat can lift you up.

slides.title: Move at every break
slides.body: At quarter-time or between games, walk a lap of the field, do a few gentle back bends with hands on hips, or swing your arms. Small, regular movement beats one big stretch later.

slides.title: Carry smarter from the car
slides.body: Eskies, chairs and kit bags add up. Split loads between both hands, keep heavy things close, and step in close to the boot with bent knees rather than reaching in.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain spreading into a leg, numbness, weakness or pain that keeps building over weeks is worth an assessment. Bladder or bowel changes or numbness around the groin need urgent medical care.
